title: Children of God and the Shape of Love
summary: John marvels at the Father's love in calling believers his children and promises that when Christ appears they will be like him. God's children do not make a practice of sin, because Christ came to take away sin and destroy the devil's works. They love one another, unlike Cain, and they learn what love is from Jesus, who laid down his life. Such love is practical, reaching the brother in need, and it gives confidence before God even when the heart condemns.
story: Chapter 2 ended with the thought of being born of God. Chapter 3 opens by celebrating what that means: the Father's love has made believers his children, now, even though what they will be has not yet been revealed. The chapter then brings together the two moral tests already introduced, righteousness and love, and grounds both in who Christ is and what he did. It prepares for chapter 4, which will return to the test of belief and then give the letter's fullest treatment of love.
historical:
The chapter's strong language about sin makes most sense against the background of the schism. Those who left the community may have claimed that their spiritual knowledge put them above ordinary moral concern, so that what one did in the body did not matter. Later Christian writers describe groups, often grouped loosely under the name Gnostics, who held either that the body was unimportant and could be indulged, or that the truly spiritual person was beyond sin altogether. We can't be sure how developed those ideas were in John's day, and it is wise not to read second-century systems back into the letter. But verse 7, let no one deceive you, suggests that someone was teaching that a person could be righteous without practicing righteousness.

The example of Cain (verse 12) is the only direct reference to an Old Testament story in the letter. Genesis 4 tells of Cain killing his brother Abel, and Jewish tradition by the first century had come to treat Cain as the model of hatred and envy. John uses him to show where hatred leads and why the world, like Cain, may hate the righteous.
cultural:
The language of children and of being born of God would have landed in a world where family identity shaped everything. A person's father determined their name, inheritance, status, and duties, and children were expected to resemble and honor their father. John draws on this: God's children resemble him in righteousness and love, while those who practice sin show the family likeness of the devil. The image of God's seed (sperma) abiding in the believer (verse 9) uses the ancient understanding of the father's seed as passing on his nature.

Verse 17's picture of someone with the world's goods seeing a brother in need would have been immediate for readers in the Roman world, where there was no public welfare, where famine and debt could quickly ruin a family, and where early Christian communities became known for caring for their own poor and widows. The word translated compassion is literally the inner organs, which ancient people regarded as the seat of the emotions: to close one's heart is, in the Greek, to shut up one's bowels.
literary: The chapter has two halves joined by the theme of the children of God. Verses 1-10 focus on righteousness and sin: God's children are pure as Christ is pure, and the one born of God does not keep on sinning. Verse 10 acts as a hinge, naming both tests: practicing righteousness and loving one's brother. Verses 11-24 then focus on love, moving from the negative example of Cain to the positive example of Christ (verse 16), then to practical love (verses 17-18) and assurance (verses 19-24). John writes in sharp contrasts: children of God and children of the devil, life and death, love and hate, word and deed. The chapter ends by introducing the Spirit as the evidence that God remains in us, a theme picked up in chapter 4.

outline.t: The Father's love: children now, like him later
God's children do not practice sin
Love one another, not like Cain
Love defined by Christ and shown in deeds
Confidence before God and the gift of the Spirit

doctrines.note: Believers are called and actually are children of God by the Father's love, a present reality with a future completion: when Christ appears, we will be like him (verse 2). Salvation includes new birth and a new family likeness.

Sin is lawlessness (verse 4), rebellion against God and not only a mistake. Christ appeared to take it away and to destroy the works of the devil, so a settled life of sin contradicts what he came to do.

The church is a family in which believers are brothers and sisters, and love for them is the mark of having passed from death to life. That love is measured by self-giving and by open-handed care for those in need.
The Spirit whom God has given is the evidence that God remains in his people (verse 24). John will develop this in chapter 4 as the Spirit who confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh.

words.note: Teknon, child, from a root associated with bearing or begetting. John prefers it to the more legal word for son (huios), which he reserves for Jesus. The choice stresses birth and family likeness: believers are God's children because they have been born of him.

Anomia, lawlessness. John defines sin as lawlessness, not merely breaking a rule but refusing God's rightful rule. The word was also associated with the rebellion expected in the last days (2 Thessalonians 2:3 speaks of the man of lawlessness), so calling all sin lawlessness exposes it as siding with the enemy.

Sperma, seed. God's seed abides in the one born of God (verse 9). Interpreters take the seed as the new divine life implanted in the believer, the Holy Spirit, or the word of God. On any reading, it is God's own life in the believer that makes a settled life of sin impossible.

christ: Christ is at the center of both halves of the chapter. He is the pure and righteous one whom God's children will one day resemble, when they see him as he is (verse 2). He appeared to take away sins, and in him there is no sin (verse 5). He was revealed to destroy the works of the devil (verse 8), a summary of his mission that joins his cross and resurrection to the defeat of evil. And his death defines love itself: by this we know what love is, that Jesus laid down his life for us (verse 16). The call to lay down our lives for one another is not an ideal in the abstract but the imitation of a person.

hard.q: How can John say that no one born of God keeps on sinning, when he also said that anyone who claims to have no sin is deceived?
hard.a:
The apparent contradiction between 1:8-10 and 3:6-9 is one of the letter's best-known puzzles. The most common answer points to the Greek present tense in chapter 3, which often signals ongoing action: the one born of God does not keep on sinning, or does not make a practice of sin, while still committing individual sins that need confession. Many translations, including the BSB, reflect that reading.

Others think grammar alone can't carry the weight and suggest that John is speaking of a particular kind of sin, the deliberate rejection of God that marked those who left, or of sin as a settled way of life, lawlessness. Still others see John speaking ideally, describing what the new birth produces in principle and what the Christian is becoming, in contrast with teachers who treated sin as unimportant. Wesleyan traditions have drawn on these verses in teaching that believers can be freed from willful sin. Across these views, the pastoral balance is John's own: do not deny your sin, and do not make peace with it.

questions: John says believers are God's children now, even though what they will be has not yet been revealed. How does that present identity shape the way you see yourself on a bad day?
Love is defined by Jesus laying down his life and shown by opening one's hand to a brother in need. Where is that kind of love being asked of you right now?
When your heart condemns you, John says that God is greater than your heart. How does that promise speak to guilt that lingers after confession?
